new_d.text: A name for positions holding that capitalism's own tendencies should be pushed further. Robin Mackay and Armen Avanessian call accelerationism “a political heresy: the insistence that the only radical political response to capitalism” is “to accelerate its uprooting, alienating, decoding, abstractive tendencies”.

new_text.text: They note that the word first appeared in Roger Zelazny's science-fiction novel Lord of Light (1967) and was taken up as a critical term by Benjamin Noys in The Persistence of the Negative (2010).

Alex Williams reports that for Noys the term covers “certain libertarian post-Marxist positions”, Deleuze and Guattari's Anti-Oedipus, Lyotard's Libidinal Economy and the Baudrillard of the mid-1970s, and quotes him: they answer Marx's claim that “the real barrier of capitalist production is capital itself” by “turning capitalism against itself”, on the principle of “the worse the better”.

Anti-Oedipus asks whether the revolutionary path is to withdraw from the world market or to go further, to “accelerate the process”, a phrase Deleuze and Guattari credit to Nietzsche; Williams writes that Nick Land “answered in the affirmative”.

David Cunningham describes a first wave, for which, he writes, Anti-Oedipus may have provided much of the vocabulary and whose most extreme form is Lyotard's Libidinal Economy (1974), and a second in the work of Land and the Cybernetic Culture Research Unit (CCRU) in the UK during the early 1990s; Noys, he reports, calls the result a “Deleuzian Thatcherism”.

Simon O'Sullivan reads Land's essay “Circuitries” as pitching positive feedback loops against the stabilizing effect of negative ones: “the call is for ever more mutation and deviation from the norm”.
Cunningham writes that Land's later writings “jettison the horizon of a non-capitalist future altogether”.

In “A Quick-and-Dirty Introduction to Accelerationism” Land describes the basic schema as “a positive feedback circuit”, in which commercialization and industrialization “mutually excite each other in a runaway process, from which modernity draws its gradient”, and writes: “Accelerationism is simply the self-awareness of capitalism, which has scarcely begun.”

Williams and Nick Srnicek's “#Accelerate: Manifesto for an Accelerationist Politics” (2013) calls for an accelerationist politics “at ease with a modernity of abstraction, complexity, globality, and technology”, and holds that the platforms of production, finance, logistics and consumption “can and will be reprogrammed and reformatted towards post-capitalist ends”.
It faults Land's “myopic yet hypnotising belief that capitalist speed alone could generate a global transition”.

Land, discussing the manifesto, holds that whatever can consistently feed socio-historical acceleration “will necessarily, or by essence, be capital”, so that the prospect of an unambiguous left accelerationism “can be confidently dismissed”.

Mackay and Avanessian's #Accelerate: The Accelerationist Reader (2014) builds, in Cunningham's words, “a kind of intellectual prehistory” for the manifesto, beginning with Marx's “Fragment on Machines” and Samuel Butler's Erewhon (1872), and its editors set “Land’s consolidated right-accelerationism” against “the burgeoning left-accelerationisms”.
Noys's Malign Velocities (2014) rejects the position and tracks accelerationism “as the symptom of the misery and pain of labour under capitalism”.

new_d.text: A term from the Cybernetic Culture Research Unit (CCRU) at Warwick in the 1990s for a fiction that makes itself real. Nick Land defines it as “a positive feedback circuit including culture as a component”.

new_text.text: Simon O'Sullivan credits Land with coining the term at the CCRU, and Alex Williams credits the CCRU.

O'Sullivan glosses the CCRU's definition as “a fiction that makes itself real through time-travelling feedback loops”, which “operates as a future vision thrown back to engineer its own history”, and quotes the group's own list: “Element of effective culture that makes itself real.” “Fictional quantity functional as a time-traveling device.” “Coincidence intensifier.” “Call to the Old Ones.”

In an interview with Delphi Carstens (2009) Land calls it “the experimental (techno-)science of self-fulfilling prophecies”: superstitions are “merely false beliefs”, while hyperstitions, “by their very existence as ideas”, “function causally to bring about their own reality”.

His examples include capitalist economics, which he calls “extremely sensitive to hyperstition”, and the fictional idea of cyberspace, which drew the investment that made it a technosocial reality; capitalism, he says, “incarnates hyperstitional dynamics at an unprecedented and unsurpassable level of intensity”.

He describes the hyperstitional object as conjured “into being by the approach taken to it”, and distinguishes this from the subjectivistic or postmodern stance that “dissolves the independent reality of the object into cognitive or semiotic structures”.
According to O'Sullivan, Sadie Plant set up the CCRU, and Land “led” it after she left academia.

He calls positive feedback loops “another name for hyperstition” and reads Land's essays of the 1990s as “time loops in which the future they predict impacts back on the present”: in “Circuitries” a science-fiction narrative accompanies the theory, and “Meat (or How to Kill Oedipus in Cyberspace)” is “both politico-philosophical treatise and cyberpunk fiction”.

He quotes the Hyperstition website, whose list opens with the Numogram, “Rigorous systematic unfolding of the Decimal Labyrinth”, and calls this work “the first great task of hyperstition”; O'Sullivan reads it as “the positing of a deep (and inhuman) numerical reality”.

Williams, writing on accelerationism in 2013, glosses hyperstition as “narratives able to effectuate their own reality through the workings of feedback loops”, and Mackay and Avanessian present their #Accelerate: The Accelerationist Reader (2014) as producing accelerationism itself “as a fictional or hyperstitional anticipation of intelligence to come”.

old.text: A necessary truth or being could not have been otherwise.
old.note: Restated with Kment's possible-worlds definitions, quoted; necessary being comes in through Spinoza's necessity 'in respect to its essence'.

old.text: A contingent one could have been otherwise, or might never have existed.
old.note: Kment's definition of contingency quoted.

old.text: Philosophers distinguish kinds of necessity: logical (denying it yields a contradiction), metaphysical (true in every possible world), physical (fixed by the laws of nature) and conditional (necessary given something else).
old.note: Kment gives truth in all possible worlds for necessity in general; metaphysical necessity he gives through Kit Fine's account (truth in virtue of natures), and nomic necessity as necessitation by the laws. Necessity by contradiction and conditional necessity are Leibniz's absolute and ex hypothesi necessity (Look, Discourse §13). Each now credited to its source.

old.text: Leibniz grounded contingent truths in God's choice of the best possible world.
old.note: Look: contingent connections rest on God's free decrees (Discourse §13), and God made the best world actual; now quoted. The Monadology §§33–46 locator was not checked against a source and is replaced by Discourse §13, which Look quotes.

old.text: Kripke argued that some necessary truths, such as “water is H₂O”, can be known only a posteriori, which pulls necessity apart from a priority.
old.note: Kment: Putnam and Kripke threw into doubt that all and only a priori truths are necessary. 'Water is H₂O' was set in quotation marks as if quoted and is in no source consulted as an example of this; replaced by one of Kment's examples, quoted.

new_d.text: A necessary truth is one that could not have been false, and a contingent truth one that is true and could have been false. In the possible-worlds terms Boris Kment sets out, a proposition is necessary “just in case it is true in all possible worlds” and contingent “just in case it is true in some but not all possible worlds”.

new_text.text: Kment separates several kinds: metaphysical necessity, which on Kit Fine's account is truth “in virtue of the natures of things”; nomic necessity, which can be defined as “the property of being metaphysically necessitated by the laws of nature” and is often assumed to be the weaker of the two; and a prioricity, which he calls epistemic necessity and “an epistemological notion”.

He writes that the idea that all and only the a priori truths are necessary was “thrown into serious doubt” by Hilary Putnam (1972) and Saul Kripke (1980); one of his examples of a necessary truth known a posteriori is “If gold exists, then it has atomic number 79.”

In F. H. Peters's translation of the Nicomachean Ethics, Aristotle holds that “The object of science, then, is necessary. Therefore it is eternal” (VI.3), and that prudence cannot be a science, because “the sphere of action is that which is alterable” and “things that are necessarily determined do not admit of deliberation” (VI.5).

Spinoza's Ethics calls a thing necessary “either in respect to its essence or in respect to its cause”, and holds that “a thing can in no respect be called contingent, save in relation to the imperfection of our knowledge” (I, Proposition 33, Note 1).
Steven Nadler sums up the result: “There are no alternatives to the actual world”, and there is “no contingency or spontaneity within the world”.

Brandon Look writes that Leibniz's philosophy can be seen as a reaction to, among other things, “the necessitarianism of Spinoza and Hobbes”, and quotes Leibniz recalling that the consideration of possibles that never exist “brought me back from this precipice”.

In the Discourse on Metaphysics (§13), as Look quotes it, a truth “whose contrary implies a contradiction is absolutely necessary”, while a contingent truth is necessary only ex hypothesi and rests on God's free decrees; according to Leibniz, God “surveyed the infinitely many possible worlds, determined which was best” and made it actual.

new_d.text: Ethics centered on character. Rosalind Hursthouse and Glen Pettigrove describe it as the approach in normative ethics “that emphasizes the virtues, or moral character”, beside deontology, which emphasizes duties or rules, and consequentialism, which emphasizes the consequences of actions.

new_text.text: They call a virtue “an excellent trait of character”: “a disposition, well entrenched in its possessor”, “to notice, expect, value, feel, desire, choose, act, and react in certain characteristic ways”.

Full virtue also needs phronesis, “moral or practical wisdom”, which “characteristically comes only with experience of life”. Among the topics the virtue ethics tradition has always taken up, they list the questions of “what sorts of persons we should be and how we should live”.
Nafsika Athanassoulis gives the advice a virtue ethicist is likely to offer as “Act as a virtuous person would act in your situation.”

Aristotle's definition, in F. H. Peters's translation: “Virtue, then, is a habit or trained faculty of choice, the characteristic of which lies in moderation or observance of the mean relatively to the persons concerned, as determined by reason, i.e. by the reason by which the prudent man would determine it” (Nicomachean Ethics II.6).

His example in the next chapter: “Moderation in the feelings of fear and confidence is courage”; an excess of confidence makes a man foolhardy, and an excess of fear makes him cowardly (II.7). Prudence is Peters's word for phronēsis.

Hursthouse and Pettigrove add that for Aristotle virtue is necessary for eudaimonia and not sufficient, since external goods are also needed, while for Plato and the Stoics it is both necessary and sufficient.

Spinoza's Ethics identifies virtue with power: “By virtue (virtus) and power I mean the same thing” (IV, Definition 8); “the foundation of virtue is the endeavour to preserve one’s own being”, and “virtue is to be desired for its own sake” (IV, Proposition 18, Note).
Steven Nadler writes that for Spinoza “Our virtue, therefore, consists in the pursuit of knowledge and understanding, of adequate ideas.” See conatus.

In the West, Hursthouse and Pettigrove write, the founders of virtue ethics are Plato and Aristotle, and in the East it can be traced back to Mencius and Confucius; it was the dominant approach in Western moral philosophy until at least the Enlightenment, was briefly eclipsed in the nineteenth century, and re-emerged in Anglo-American philosophy in the late 1950s, heralded by Anscombe's “Modern Moral Philosophy” (1958), which “crystallized an increasing dissatisfaction with the forms of deontology and utilitarianism then prevailing”.

The Internet Encyclopedia's entry on Alasdair MacIntyre calls After Virtue (1981) his best-known book and reports its argument that “an Aristotelian ethics of virtue may remain possible” without appeal to Aristotle's metaphysics of nature.
